nameStory: The "redwhisker" part of this plant's name comes from its striking reddish-purple stamens that stick way out beyond the white petals, looking like colorful whiskers on a cat's face. The "clammyweed" part becomes obvious the moment you touch it – the sticky, glandular hairs covering the stems will leave your hands feeling noticeably clammy and gooey. It's one of those plants where the common name tells you exactly what you're in for!
description: Redwhisker clammyweed is an annual wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall in sandy, disturbed areas throughout New England. It's most recognizable for its small white flowers with long, bright reddish-purple stamens that extend far beyond the petals like whiskers. The plant has a bushy, upright growth habit with sticky stems and three-part leaves, and it produces slender upward-pointing seed capsules. Fair warning – it has a distinctly unpleasant, sulfur-like smell when you get close!

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four white or cream petals about an inch long with numerous reddish-purple stamens extending well beyond the petals like colorful whiskers. The stamens are unequal lengths, giving a spiky, wild appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves made of three oval leaflets arranged like a clover, each leaflet about an inch long. The leaves feel slightly sticky to the touch due to glandular hairs.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Covered in sticky glandular hairs that will leave your fingers feeling clammy and gooey after touching. The stems have a strong, unpleasant sulfur-like odor when crushed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender capsules 1-2 inches long that point upward from the stem, containing small reddish-brown seeds. The upward orientation is distinctive compared to related species.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy annual plant 1-3 feet tall with flowers arranged in elongated clusters at the stem tips. Thrives in sandy, gravelly, or disturbed soils in full sun.

habitat: Look for redwhisker clammyweed in sandy, gravelly, or highly disturbed soils where few other plants can thrive – think roadsides, construction sites, gravel pits, and sandy shorelines. It loves full sun and tolerates dry conditions, often appearing as one of the few plants growing in seemingly barren, poor soils. You're most likely to find it in areas with little competition from other vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up. Young plants develop their characteristic three-part leaves and begin growing their sticky, glandular stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with white flowers and prominent red whisker-like stamens appearing from June through August. The strong sulfur smell is most noticeable during hot summer days.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering into early fall (through October) while simultaneously producing upward-pointing seed capsules. Plants begin to look scraggly and may start dying back after first frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil. No above-ground parts persist through winter months.

funFact: The scientific name literally means "many unequal twelve" – 'polys anisos dodecandra' – because while the species name suggests 12 stamens, the plant actually has many stamens of unequal lengths, making each flower look like a tiny firework exploding with red whiskers!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its close relative spider flower (Cleome), which has similar white petals and long stamens. The key difference: redwhisker clammyweed's seed pods point upward like little rockets, while spider flower pods hang down or stick out sideways. Remember: "clammyweed climbs up, cleome cascades down."
contextualKnowledge: Despite the unappetizing name "clammyweed" and its sulfurous smell, this native plant is actually quite beneficial for disturbed ecosystems, helping stabilize poor soils where other plants struggle. The sticky hairs that make it "clammy" are actually specialized glandular structures that may help protect the plant from insects and reduce water loss.
compareHints: Redwhisker clammyweed is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England. Compared to its closest relative spider flower (Cleome) in the same family, clammyweed is generally smaller, has more compact flower clusters, and most distinctively has seed capsules that point upward rather than drooping downward. The "clammy" sticky texture is also more pronounced than in spider flower.
